main_text.l: Probatio Divisionis.
Si autem scire cupio an recte primum ex-
emplum diviserim, abjicio 9 a quoto in se-
micirculo, & 5 remanent, quae ad dextrum la-
tus literæ X colloco, & Divisorem, nempe 3
ad sinistrum latus scribo, dices: Ter 5. sunt 15, 5
& 1 sunt 6, q; supra X noto. Deinde abjicio 9
a Dividendo, & remanent
6, q; sub X noto.
[Division proof diagram: the cross-multiplication scheme of the first example, with the numbers (18104 and the quotient 3, 6, 5, 6 arranged around an X-shaped cross]
Exemplum cum duobus Divisoribus sic
probo: Abjicio 9 a Quoto, & 2 quae rema-
nent, ad dextrum latus literæ X noto, &
Divisores per additionē conjungo, dicens:
1 & 2 sunt 3, ter bina vel bis terna sunt 6, qui-
bus residuum, nempe 3 addo, & sunt 9: Et
scribo o supra X. Deinde abjicio 9 a Divi-
dendo, & remanet o, quam sub X colloco.
Sed huic Regulæ non nimiū confidendum;
quia, ut nonnulli experti sunt, sæpè fallit.
[Division proof diagram: the cross-multiplication scheme of the second example, with the numbers (3 and (470 and the quotient 3, 2, 0 arranged around an X-shaped cross]

page.notes: The two worked division proofs are diagrams of casting-out-nines calculations with small symbols (crosses, dots, circles) that cannot be fully reproduced as text; the diagram lines are descriptions, not transcription. The printed numerals in the diagrams are (18104 and (470, with quotient digits 3,6,5,6 and 3,2,0 respectively. The "q;" forms are printed abbreviations for -que and are kept as printed. "nimiū" is printed with a macron over u. Long s is rendered as s throughout.
